newsitem.title: AUSTRIA: FOCUS - Creditanstalt saga goes into extra time.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Creditanstalt saga goes into extra time.

text.p: The seemingly endless saga of the privatisation of Creditanstalt went into another round on Friday when savings bank Die Erste said agreement over a final offer for Austria's flagship bank was still a long way off.
"Even though we have made good progress in our talks, some major issues are still open," a spokesman for Die Erste Oesterreichische Spar-Casse Bank AG told Reuters.

Die Erste originally proposed to set up a joint holding company for Creditanstalt-Bankverein which would hold 74.9 percent of Die Erste's shares and all of Creditanstalt's. But talks with its consortium partners have been mired in problems for several weeks now.

The group, billed as the "Austrian solution" in the six-year history of unsuccesful attempts to privatise Creditanstalt, includes insurer EA-Generali AG, Germany's Commerzbank AG, Banca Commerciale Italiana SpA and several smaller Austrian companies.

Die Erste's spokesman said there were major disagreements within the consortium over the savings bank's exact weight in the proposed holding structure and how voting power should be distributed between its constituents.

Die Erste said negotiations would have to continue for at least several more days, if not weeks, and that it could not comply with the government's demand to receive a final offer for its 70 percent voting stake in the bank by Friday.
The news helped to push Creditanstalt's preferred shares to a new year-low of 470.30 schillings in an overall buoyant Vienna market.
Finance Minister Viktor Klima, in charge of the sale, refrained from comment, but a source close to him made scant attempts to hide the minister's disappointment.
"Maybe they're about to come out with something. Maybe a miracle will happen," the source told Reuters.
He added Klima, eager to use an estimated 18 billion schillings ($1.73 billion) in revenue from the sale to prop up the government's ailing finances, was likely to extend the deadline.

Putting a new spin on the controversy among the consortium, Die Erste said it had proposed to increase its weight in the planned holding. "We are now offering to put in a substantial amount of cash (on top of the 74.9 percent of shares) in order to safeguard Austrian interests," the spokesman said.
"Because Die Erste is the Austrian bank partner in this consortium we feel we have a special responsibility," he added.

Creditanstalt executives have given Die Erste's plans the cold shoulder because they fear it would give the savings bank undue influence over Creditanstalt, Austria's second-largest bank with assets of almost 700 billion schillings. Die Erste is less than a third the size of Creditanstalt.
But Die Erste, together with its partners, is the only known bidder for Creditanstalt, founded by the Rothschild family in 1863 and former banker to the Habsburg dynasty.

The government has long said it wanted to sell its stake in Creditanstalt, widely regarded as the gem of the Alpine republic's overcrowded banking sector, in a way that "safeguards Austrian interests".

Several international suitors, among them Allianz AG of Germany and CS Holding of Switzerland, over the past years have been scared away by what they saw as a bias against foreigners in Austria's leading political circles. ($1=10.40 Schilling)
